rv.q: The everyday poison known as toxic masculinity becomes dangerously easy
Linda Vista doesn’t let anyone off the hook that easily, and if there’s hope to be had, it won’t come cheap.
Linda Vista is a funny, sad, smart and sprawling portrait of middle-aged male disappointment that feels both bracingly honest and somewhat indulgent.
Linda Vista is lovely, funny, and sad, and I'm dreading the day when it becomes a sitcom.
Don't let the slick barrage of one-liners deceive you into thinking there's no room here for bruising self-examination and perhaps even tentative growth.
“Linda Vista” really is that good.
The dialogue is razor sharp and positively laced with laughter—the kind of laughter that comes not merely from “funny” lines but innocent lines that are funny in context.
Whatever your view, the play is hilarious, real, poignant and recognizable, and adds luster to Tracy Letts’ continuing output.
Luckily, Letts’ razor-sharp skill at dialogue and characterization will keep most of us riveted, even when we’re feeling angry, disgusted or just a little sad.
Linda Vista makes a strong argument that we cannot see the beautiful view when we're too preoccupied with trying to take the best selfie in front of it.

Indeed, your ability to get past that question – and, more generally, your willingness to entertain yet another middle-aged white guy comedy – is a gauge of how much you will appreciate this showcase for some impressive acting and very funny writing.

That’s at once Linda Vista’s greatest truth and flaw: a major character who we grow to love, but ultimately can’t believe in.
Unfortunately, the play gets entangled in its own repetitive pattern and piles on dysfunction upon dysfunction without any hint at resolution.
After letting the character loose with his stand-up routine in the first act, the playwright turns Wheeler into a horny bore in the second act.
He’s a heterosexual disaster zone, and one which the playwright (and by extension us) end up feeling a little too ambivalent about.
As central characters go, Wheeler is, admittedly, supremely unlikable.

But, as embraced by director Dexter Bullard, it plays like one of those formulaic, comfortably predictable sitcoms that you might have enjoyed twenty years ago, but watching it now makes you cringe at what you once found funny.
Barford, uninhibited and honest, is perfectly cast and leads a uniformly very fine ensemble
Linda Vista feels like an intensely personal play for Letts, by turns howlingly funny and deeply unsettling.
He may be a liberal, loud mouthed and self righteous, but he is one difficult Dick to be around.

The entire cast is remarkable, and Mr. Barford certainly turns in an impressive performance but at times the content diminishes the vulnerability of Wheeler, leaving only an angry, despicable, incorrigible moron with no redeeming values.
No surprise then, that it's dramatically DOA.

cn.t: Letts' darkly funny midlife-crisis comedy earns praise for sharp dialogue and Ian Barford's superb performance, though critics divide on whether its toxic male protagonist merits nearly three hours of stage time.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.
